findings.title: SafeParse wrapper object is stored as the credential key, corrupting Google Calendar credentials
findings.body: In refreshAccessToken, `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema)` returns the full zod SafeParse result (`{ success: true, data: {...} }`), not the parsed credentials. This object is then written to the DB via `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`. The previous code stored `googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials)` (the unwrapped data). After the very first token refresh, the credential's key in the database becomes `{"success":true,"data":{...}}`, and every subsequent construction of GoogleCalendarService fails at `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` in googleAuth, permanently breaking Google Calendar for that credential until the row is manually fixed. This affects all users, not just those with credential syncing enabled.

findings.title: prisma is used but never imported in salesforce CalendarService
findings.body: The newly added code calls `await prisma.credential.update({ where: { id: credential.id }, ... })` in getClient, but the file's import list (lines 1-20) contains no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`. This is a compile-time error (Cannot find name 'prisma') and will break the type-check/build for the whole app-store package.

findings.title: Sync branch returns a raw fetch Response while callers expect provider-specific parsed bodies
findings.body: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, refreshOAuthTokens returns the raw fetch `Response`. In the fallback branch it returns whatever the provider-specific refreshFunction returns (an axios response for zoho apps, a Gaxios response for Google, a token object for HubSpot, a fetch Response for office365/lark/zoom). Callers that don't expect a fetch Response break when sync is enabled: HubSpot reads `.expiresIn`/`.accessToken` off the Response and stores the Response object itself as the credential key; zoho-bigin and zohocrm dereference `tokenInfo.data.error` on the Response (`data` is undefined) and crash with a TypeError; Google reads `res?.data` which is undefined. The return-type contract of this helper is inconsistent and silently breaks most integrations in sync mode.

findings.title: With sync enabled, HubSpot credential key is overwritten with a serialized fetch Response
findings.body: When credential sync is enabled, refreshOAuthTokens returns a raw fetch Response, so `hubspotRefreshToken` is a Response object. `hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn` is undefined, making `expiryDate` NaN, and then `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key: hubspotRefreshToken as any } })` JSON-serializes the Response (effectively `{}`) into the credential key, permanently destroying the user's stored HubSpot tokens. `hubspotClient.setAccessToken(hubspotRefreshToken.accessToken)` also sets an undefined token, so subsequent HubSpot API calls fail. The credential row must be manually repaired afterwards.

findings.title: credentialId is passed to the sync endpoint instead of userId
findings.body: refreshOAuthTokens is called as `refreshOAuthTokens(fn, "zoho-bigin", credentialId)` where the third parameter is `userId: number | null` and is sent to the self-hoster's sync endpoint as `calcomUserId`. Passing the credential id means the external app store will look up (and return) tokens for the wrong user — either a failure or, worse, another user's Bigin tokens stored on this user's credential. Every other integration passes `credential.userId`; this one should too.

findings.title: Google refresh silently no-ops when credential sync is enabled
findings.body: In sync mode refreshOAuthTokens returns a raw fetch Response, so `const token = res?.data` is undefined and `token.access_token` throws a TypeError. The catch block treats any message other than "invalid_grant" as recoverable and just returns the auth client with the stale, expired credentials. The result: with sync enabled, Google Calendar token refresh never succeeds, the new tokens are never used or stored, and the failure is completely silent — all calendar API calls then fail with expired-token errors.

findings.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema's computed keys are nonsense — the schema only validates access_token and strips the expiry
findings.body: `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional()` do not create catch-all keys: `z.string().toString()` evaluates to the string "[object Object]", so both computed keys collapse to a single literal property named "[object Object]". The schema therefore only requires `access_token` and — because zod strips unknown keys — drops every other field, including the expiry that the comment says is being captured. Downstream consequences when sync is enabled: office365calendar never updates its stored expiry (token is re-fetched on every API call), zoom stores expiry_date NaN, and office365video sets expiry_date to Date.now() (immediately expired).

findings.title: Placeholder string "refresh_token" overwrites real refresh tokens in the database
findings.body: When the (sync) response has no refresh_token, the code sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. Callers then persist this: office365calendar merges tokenResponse.data into the stored key (line 264 of office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts) and zoom copies `newTokens.refresh_token` into the stored key (line 120 of zoomvideo/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts). The user's real OAuth refresh token is thus permanently replaced by the literal string "refresh_token", so if sync is ever disabled or the fallback path runs, the credential can no longer be refreshed and the integration is dead until re-connected.

findings.title: Bigin token refresh crashes with TypeError when credential sync is enabled
findings.body: In sync mode refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response, which has no `.data` property, so `if (!tokenInfo.data.error)` throws "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'error')". The same pattern exists in zohocrm/lib/CalendarService.ts line 217 (`zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error`). Token refresh for both Zoho apps is therefore guaranteed to throw whenever APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set.

findings.title: Webex refresh rejects sync-endpoint responses because it still validates against the full Webex schema
findings.body: Unlike the other apps, webex was not migrated to parseRefreshTokenResponse: it still runs `webexRefreshedTokenSchema.safeParse(responseBody)`, which requires scope/token_type/refresh_token/refresh_token_expires_in. When sync is enabled, the request is redirected to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT, whose documented response contains only the access token and expiry, so the parse always fails and refreshAccessToken rejects with "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned". Webex video is therefore completely broken for any instance that enables credential sync.

findings.title: Zoom sync path stores placeholder refresh token and NaN expiry_date
findings.body: In sync mode, parseRefreshTokenResponse uses the minimal schema, so newTokens contains only access_token plus the placeholder `refresh_token: "refresh_token"`. The code then does `key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token` (overwriting the real refresh token with the placeholder) and `key.expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + newTokens.expires_in * 1000)` where expires_in is undefined, producing NaN, which is written to the Json column (JSON-serializes to null or throws depending on the Prisma version). The stored Zoom credential is corrupted after the first synced refresh.

findings.title: MS Teams sync path stores a key without refresh_token and with an already-expired expiry_date
findings.body: When sync is enabled, responseBody is the sync endpoint's JSON (access token + expiry only). The code then computes `expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + (responseBody?.expires_in || 0) * 1000)`, i.e. the current time, so the token is immediately considered expired and every meeting creation triggers another sync request. Worse, `key: responseBody` replaces the entire stored credential key, permanently discarding the saved refresh_token — after the next server restart the in-memory copy is gone and the credential can never be refreshed through the normal path again.

findings.title: Office365 expiry is never updated in sync mode, causing a sync-endpoint call on every calendar operation
findings.body: In sync mode parseRefreshTokenResponse returns only `{ access_token }` (unknown keys stripped, expiry never captured). The merge `{ ...o365AuthCredentials, ...tokenResponse.data }` therefore keeps the old, already-expired `expires_in` epoch value. Since getToken checks `!isExpired(o365AuthCredentials.expires_in)`, the freshly synced token is still considered expired, so every single Graph API call (availability, event create/update/delete) triggers a new POST to the sync endpoint. It also removed the previous logging of zod errors, making misconfigurations harder to diagnose.

findings.title: Refreshed Salesforce token is stored but the client is built with the stale access token
findings.body: getClient fetches a fresh token set and writes it to the DB, but then constructs the jsforce.Connection with `accessToken: credentialKey.access_token` — the old, possibly expired token from before the refresh. The new access token (`accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`) is never used. Additionally, this refresh fetch now runs unconditionally on every service instantiation (previously jsforce refreshed lazily only when needed), adding a blocking Salesforce round-trip to every calendar operation, and when APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is set the minimal parse schema strips fields like instance_url, so the stored key loses data needed for future connections.

findings.title: Decrypted keys are stored without any validation against the app's expected key shape
findings.body: The webhook decrypts `keys` and writes the parsed JSON directly into credential.key with no validation against the per-app credential schema (e.g. zoomTokenSchema, googleCredentialSchema). If the self-hoster's app sends malformed or incomplete keys (wrong field names, missing refresh token), the credential is created/updated successfully but every service that does `schema.parse(credential.key)` will throw at runtime, breaking that user's integration with no indication of why. At minimum the payload should be validated against the app's key schema before persisting.

findings.title: findFirst-then-create/update race allows duplicate credentials
findings.body: The handler does `prisma.credential.findFirst({ userId, appId })` and then creates a new credential if none was found. Two webhook deliveries arriving concurrently for the same user/app will both observe no existing credential and both create one, leaving duplicate credentials for the same app. Downstream code uses findFirst and silently ignores the duplicates. There is no unique constraint on (userId, appId) to back this up, so the upsert should be made atomic (e.g. a transaction with locking or a unique constraint).

findings.title: Webhook secret compared with a non-constant-time string comparison
findings.body: `req.headers[...] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` uses a plain inequality check, which short-circuits on the first differing byte and is susceptible to timing analysis. Since this secret is the only thing protecting an endpoint that writes third-party OAuth credentials into the database, it should be compared with a constant-time comparison (e.g. crypto.timingSafeEqual on equal-length buffers).

findings.title: Unhandled ZodError/decryption failures and no HTTP method check produce 500s
findings.body: The handler doesn't restrict the HTTP method and calls `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` and `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` without a try/catch. A GET request, a malformed body, or an incorrectly encrypted `keys` payload throws an unhandled exception, returning an opaque 500 instead of a 400/401 with a useful message, which will make webhook misconfigurations hard for self-hosters to debug.
